newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Cocoa gains while coffee and metals lag.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Cocoa gains while coffee and metals lag.

text.p: Strong gains in cocoa on Monday placed it head and shoulders above lacklustre metals and weak coffee as these markets cooled off after last week's price swings.
London cocoa prices rose to a spectacular 4-1/2 month high in a driven by short covering on news from the leading producer Ivory Coast, traders said.
The benchmark May contract gained 35 stg to close at 981 stg.
Ivorian commodities minister, Alain Gauze told an International Cocoa Organisation (ICCO) meeting the country had no more cocoa to sell.
He said the government would destroy all illegally-planted coffee and cocoa which would leave the 1996/97 crop between 900,000 and 950,000 tonnes - undershooting forecasts.
Around 800,000 tonnes have already been sold.
The market responded quickly. "Cocoa has risen by 100 stg from the lows," said one trader. "It's all about speculative short-covering."
The ICCO meeting also heard that Ghana had sold around 200,000 tonnes of its main crop cocoa - two thirds of the total forecast for 1996/97

Coffee prices, however, showed no sign of recovering from their recent bearish tone. London's benchmark robusta futures for May delivery ended at $1,718, down $11 on the day, after touching a low of $1,699 at the open.
Dealers reported scant trading volume as sellers turned cautious after three days of straight losses.
Prices have fallen steadily from a nine-month peak last Wednesday which prompted several roasters to raise retail prices. But dealers remained optimistic over the long-term.
"Broadly speaking, coffee remains in the medium-term uptrend and any short-term weakness should be viewed as corrective," said Adrian Haylor, analyst at Sucden.
Trading was subdued on the London Metal Exchange (LME) as copper led other base metals lower.

Copper futures eased in thin volume to close at $2,358 per tonne, compared to $2,389 on Friday. Traders said buying interest was sketchy in the wake of Friday's explosive rally which ended in a sell-off and a price plunge at the close.
Aluminium mirrored copper's bearish tone, and continued its weakness after a smaller than expected warehouse stock fall of 1,800 tonnes on Friday.
LME three-month contracts closed at $1,657, down from $1,674 on Friday.
Copper dealers were watching for signs of China entering the market after the China Daily's Business Weekly said on Sunday that China's demand for copper would reach 1.2 million tonnes in 1997.
The country produced over 900,000 tonnes of the red metal last year.
But Chinese traders ruled out any activity in the immediate future, saying prices were too high to justify buying.
A Shanghai Metal Exchange source said sky-high world copper prices were not supported by fundamentals.

"I don't really see any support for $2,400," he said. "If the price can go above $2,400 a tonne and stay there for a decent period, that would indicate some support, but I think the funds are under pressure to sell."
Among the softs, soybean futures rallied to contract highs on the Chicago Board of Trade.
Traders reported heavy fund buying amid speculation the U.S. Agriculture Department would cut its 1996-97 ending stock projection in its report due on Tuesday.
Prices were pushed up by July/November spread trading, with the July premium supported by supply concerns.
Sugar was also up after Fiji Sugar Corp confirmed fears that the 130-mph cyclone which lashed the South Pacific nation last week had damaged the crop.
Before the cyclone, Fiji's 1997 raw sugar production had been forecast at 473,000 tonnes.

Precious metals, like the industrials, were mostly bearish. Gold prices lacked direction, closing up $2 from Friday at $350.50 per tonne, but were still depressed after last week's news that the Swiss Central Bank planned to sell some of its gold reserves.
Dealers said the market was still skittish, but physical demand had pushed prices up slightly.
Platinum and silver were also weak, but palladium closed higher, with traders still watching for news on the threatened strike by workers at Russia'a Norilsk Nickel complex.
Crude oil was down, with benchmark Brent April futures down to $19.56 per barrel at 1740 GMT from Friday's surge above $20.
